title: Wine tannins: Where are they coming from? A method to access the importance of berry part on wine tannins content
author: Rousserie, Lacampagne, et al.

steps.title: Determine sampling time points
steps.instruction: Identify four sampling moments for each modality (berry, seed, skin wine): (i) half alcoholic fermentation when density reaches 1.030, (ii) end of alcoholic fermentation when density reaches 0.990, (iii) middle of post‑fermentative maceration ≈ one week after the end of alcoholic fermentation, and (iv) end of post‑fermentative maceration ≈ two weeks after the end of alcoholic fermentation.

steps.title: Collect wine sample
steps.instruction: At each identified sampling moment, withdraw 20 mL of wine from the fermenter.

steps.title: Remove corresponding vegetal material
steps.instruction: Immediately after withdrawing the wine, remove from the fermenter the amount of vegetal material that corresponds to the sampled juice to keep the vegetal‑material‑to‑juice ratio constant: for the berry modality remove berries, for the seed modality remove seeds, and for the skin modality remove skins.

steps.title: Calculate vegetal material mass
steps.instruction: Compute the mass of vegetal material taken using the formula given in the article: Vegetalmaterialweight = Totalamountofvegetalmaterialinfermenter900×20.

description: To validate the method, the experiments have been conducted three times at three different maturity stages: under-ripeness, commercial ripeness and over-ripeness. The fermentation kinetics of all the experiments have been modeled. The results of density determinations during alcoholic fermentation for each modality are presented in Fig. 3.Fig. 3Fermentation kinetics for each type of wine at the three ripeness degrees.Fig. 3 For each type of wines (seed wine, skin wine and berry wine) the duplicate (try 1 and try 2) present the same fermentation kinetics. To go further, for each ripeness stages (under-ripeness, ripeness and over ripeness), fermentations of both seed, skin and berry wines are comparable:•For the under-ripeness modality, for all the type of wines, fermentations were completed on 18 days;•For the ripeness modality, for all the type of wines, fermentations were completed on 22 days;•For the over-ripeness modality, for all the type of wines, fermentations were completed on 34 days. The difference of alcoholic fermentation time between the three ripeness stages is related to the sugar composition of grape juice. Indeed, at the under-ripeness stage the sugar content was lower than the one of the over-ripeness stage. To sum up, it seems that the winemaking and the sampling methods do not affect the successful completion of the alcoholic fermentation, which allows us to validate the method.
